title: Something Flew Into My Eye

patient.name: Mr Koh Teck Guan
patient.presenting_complaint: Felt something fly into his right eye while sanding wood about an hour ago — eye is red, watery, and feels like there's grit in it

history.hpc: Mr Koh was sanding a piece of wood without goggles when he felt a small particle hit his right eye about an hour ago. Since then, the eye has been watering, red, and feels like there is sand or grit under the upper lid. He describes the discomfort as moderate (5/10), worse on blinking. He has not noticed any drop in vision. No history of a high-velocity metal-on-metal mechanism (he was using a manual sanding block, not a power grinder), so a penetrating injury is less likely.
history.pmhx: Nil significant. No previous eye conditions. Tetanus vaccination up to date (had a booster 3 years ago after a workplace cut).
history.social_hx: Carpenter by trade. Came in alone on his motorbike.

examination_findings.anterior_segment: Right eye: conjunctival hyperaemia, mild watering, a small particle of wood dust visible on the superior bulbar conjunctiva/under the upper lid on eversion. Cornea appears intact, no visible full-thickness defect or irregular pupil. Left eye: normal.

investigations.va_distance: RE: LogMAR 0.2 (6/9.5), slightly reduced likely due to watering and irritation. LE: LogMAR 0.0 (6/6).
investigations.external_inspection: Wood particle visualised on superior conjunctiva under everted upper lid. No signs of penetrating injury (pupil round and reactive, cornea appears intact).
investigations.fluorescein_staining: To be performed by doctor to check for corneal abrasion once foreign body is addressed

diagnosis: Corneal/conjunctival foreign body (wood dust particle), right eye, non-penetrating. Triage Category 3 — within 60 minutes.

immediate: Take a focused history: mechanism of injury, type of material, whether protective eyewear was worn, time since injury
Ask about tetanus status — relevant for any eye trauma
Examine the eye including lid eversion to look for a subtarsal foreign body — visualise the wood particle
Do NOT attempt to remove the foreign body yourself unless trained and authorised — refer to doctor/nurse for removal
Assign Triage Category 3 — within 60 minutes (foreign body, non-penetrating, painful but stable)
Document findings: location of foreign body, VA, and mechanism of injury
follow_up: Doctor/nurse to remove the foreign body using appropriate technique (e.g. moistened cotton bud)
Fluorescein staining to check for corneal abrasion after removal
Topical antibiotic ointment/drops may be prescribed to prevent infection while the corneal surface heals
Advise patient to return if pain worsens, vision drops, or photophobia develops
patient_education: Explain that the gritty sensation is from the wood particle and will improve once it is removed
Advise him not to rub the eye, which could cause a corneal abrasion or push the particle further in
Strongly advise wearing safety goggles when sanding or doing similar work in future
Explain that some residual scratchy feeling after removal is normal and should settle within a day or two with treatment

key_points: Establishes mechanism, material, and time of injury (wood dust, sanding, ~1 hour ago)
Asks about pain severity and any vision change
Considers and reasonably excludes a higher-velocity penetrating mechanism based on the history
Performs lid eversion to check for a subtarsal foreign body
Visualises and documents the location of the foreign body
Does not attempt removal beyond scope — refers to doctor/nurse for removal and fluorescein staining
Identifies this as a non-penetrating corneal/conjunctival foreign body
Differentiates this from a penetrating injury (Category 1) based on history and examination
Recognises the need for fluorescein staining to assess for an associated abrasion
Refers foreign body removal to appropriately trained staff
Documents mechanism, location, and findings clearly
Gives practical occupational safety advice (protective eyewear)
